content: Micafungin is an antifungal medication belonging to the echinocandin class, commonly marketed under the brand name Mycamine. It is primarily used to treat a variety of fungal infections, including candidemia, acute disseminated candidiasis, Candida peritonitis, abscesses, and esophageal candidiasis. Additionally, it is indicated for the prophylaxis of Candida infections in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). The drug is administered intravenously, typically once daily over a one-hour infusion period. Dosage and treatment duration depend on the patient’s medical condition and response to therapy. For example, treatment durations for micafungin infusions range from 6 to 51 days, with a mean duration of 19 days for certain conditions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends echinocandins, such as micafungin, as first-line therapy for Candida auris infections. Micafungin interacts with hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism, which can increase the levels or effects of several drugs, including lonafarnib, atogepant, avapritinib, axitinib, ivacaftor, lemborexant, lomitapide, midazolam (intranasal), nifedipine, sirolimus, tazemetostat, tinidazole, and ruxolitinib. These interactions necessitate caution, close monitoring, or dosage adjustments to avoid adverse effects. For instance, coadministration with lomitapide should not exceed a daily dose of 30 mg, and lemborexant’s nightly dose may need to be reduced. Micafungin also decreases the effects of Saccharomyces boulardii and may reduce the activity of probiotics when used with systemic or oral antifungals. Patients receiving micafungin should be monitored for potential side effects, including abdominal pain, anemia, headache, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, pruritus, pyrexia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and phlebitis. Serious adverse reactions, such as anaphylaxis, hemolytic anemia, hepatic impairment, renal failure, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, have been reported. Liver function abnormalities, including hepatitis and hepatic failure, have occurred in some patients, particularly those with underlying conditions or on multiple concomitant medications. Renal function abnormalities, such as elevated BUN and creatinine levels, have also been observed. Micafungin is contraindicated for intravenous bolus administration and should be infused over one hour. It is not effective against fungi other than Candida. The drug may cause fetal harm based on animal studies, and its safety in pregnant or breastfeeding women is not well established. Micafungin has been detected in the milk of lactating rats, suggesting the potential for presence in human milk. Proper storage and handling of micafungin are essential. Reconstituted or diluted solutions can be stored at controlled room temperature for up to 24 hours and must be protected from light. Patients should complete the full prescribed course of treatment, even if symptoms improve early, to ensure the infection is fully eradicated. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, including to other echinocandins, and provide a complete list of medications they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. Regular monitoring of liver and kidney function, as well as complete blood counts, is recommended during therapy. In case of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. This medication should only be used under the guidance of a healthcare professional, and patients should consult their doctor or pharmacist for any concerns or questions regarding its use.
